fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I was there in a pretty interesting window. This was 2017 into 2018, and OpenAI at that point was still fairly small. I came straight out of my PhD at MIT, where I'd been working on reinforcement learning for language, text-based games, that kind of thing, and OpenAI was really an RL shop at the time. The big bets were Dota, robotics, the dexterity work. Language was a very small corner of the building.

What struck me first was just how little friction there was between having an idea and trying it. In academia, you spend a lot of time writing proposals, waiting for compute, justifying why something deserves a GPU. There, if Alec Radford wanted to train a bigger model on more text, he mostly just did it. That sounds trivial but it changes how you think. You stop asking "can I afford to run this" and start asking "what's the actual question."

The other thing was the people. It was a dense concentration of folks who were genuinely optimistic about scaling in a way that I'd say most of the NLP community wasn't yet. I remember being a bit skeptical myself. My instinct from grad school was that you needed structure, inductive biases, task-specific architectures. And here was Alec with this sentiment neuron result, where a language model trained on Amazon reviews just happened to learn a unit that tracked sentiment, and Ilya basically saying, look, this is the direction, keep pushing it. The GPT work came out of that. It was a small team, Alec driving most of it, Tim Salimans, Ilya, and me helping on the fine-tuning and evaluation side, figuring out how to actually test whether the pretrained representations transferred across tasks.

Culturally it was a very different thing from a university lab. Less hierarchy, more of a sense that you were all pointed at the same thing. There was also less of the publication treadmill, which was freeing but also a little disorienting for someone who'd just spent five years optimizing for conference deadlines. People cared about results, and they cared about whether something would still matter in three years, more than whether it would get into the next ACL.

I'll say honestly that it wasn't obvious at the time how big that line of work would become. We thought it was a nice result. We didn't think we were naming a lineage. But the environment itself, that combination of ambition, resources, and a willingness to be wrong about conventional wisdom, that was the part that stuck with me, and it's something I've tried to recreate a little bit in my own group at Princeton, within the limits of what a university can do.

opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it was a really interesting time to be there. I joined in 2017, right after finishing my PhD at MIT, and OpenAI was very different from what people picture today. It was still a fairly small nonprofit, and it felt much more like a research lab than a company. There weren't really products to think about. The question was just: what are the big bets that could move the field?

What stood out to me most was the freedom, combined with a real willingness to try ambitious, somewhat unconventional things. In academia, especially as a grad student, you're often optimizing for the next paper and choosing problems you can finish in a few months. At OpenAI there was more appetite for "let's scale this up and see what happens," even if it wasn't obvious it would work. You also had access to compute that most university labs just didn't have back then, and that changes what questions you can even ask.

It was also very collaborative and fairly flat. You'd have people coming from very different backgrounds, some from classic ML research, some from hardcore engineering, sitting in the same room and arguing about ideas. A lot of the lab's attention at the time was on reinforcement learning, things like games and robotics. Language was a smaller effort. So working on the GPT project with Alec Radford and others felt almost like a side bet at first. Alec had this strong intuition that generative pre-training on lots of unlabeled text would give you representations that transfer, and my background was in NLP and language understanding, so it was a nice fit.

The other thing I took away was how much engineering matters. There was a lot of respect for people who could make things actually run at scale, and I think that culture, treating engineering as a first-class part of research, is a big reason a lot of those early ideas panned out. That's something I've tried to bring with me to Princeton, even though the resources in academia are obviously very different.

r001.rationale: The response describes OpenAI as a small nonprofit that felt like a research lab and says it had compute most university labs lacked, conveying a well-resourced research environment.

fable-5.text:
It was a really unique place, honestly. I was there for about a year — this was 2017, so quite early days, before OpenAI was the household name it is now. It was a pretty small organization at the time, maybe on the order of fifty, sixty people, and it had this interesting mix of feeling like an academic lab and a startup at the same time.

What struck me most was the freedom combined with the resources. In academia, you have a lot of intellectual freedom, but you're often constrained by compute, by funding cycles, by the need to publish on a regular cadence. At OpenAI, if you had a compelling idea and could convince a few people it was worth pursuing, you could just go after it, and you had access to compute that most university labs could only dream of. That combination is rarer than people think.

The other thing was the density of talent and the ambition level. People there genuinely believed they were working toward something big — this was before the scaling era had really been validated, so a lot of it was conviction rather than evidence. The GPT work actually came out of that environment. Alec Radford had been pushing on generative pre-training of language models, and there was this willingness to just scale things up and see what happened, even when the conventional wisdom in NLP at the time was much more about task-specific architectures and clever inductive biases. I remember when we were getting the results on downstream tasks, there was some skepticism from the broader community about whether this was really the right path. Internally, though, there was a real openness to betting on simple methods plus scale.

It was also quite collaborative and flat. You could walk over and talk to anyone — Ilya, the robotics folks, the RL people — and ideas crossed between groups pretty freely. Coming from a PhD environment at MIT, where research is often more siloed by advisor and group, that was refreshing. I think a lot of what I took back to Princeton, in terms of how I run my own group, was shaped by seeing how productive that kind of environment can be when you get the ingredients right.

r001.rationale: The response describes OpenAI as having abundant compute and a mix of academic lab and startup qualities, but does not mention its nonprofit status or characterize it as well-funded despite that status.

opus-5.text:
It was a really special time, honestly. When I joined it was still pretty small — on the order of fifty, sixty people, everyone in one office space in the Mission. And the thing that struck me coming out of a PhD was how little structure there was, in the best sense. There was no manager telling you what project to work on, no roadmap handed down. You'd show up, talk to people at lunch, and projects would kind of self-assemble out of those conversations. The GPT work came out of exactly that — Alec had been playing with language modeling, I'd been working on language and RL, and it was just, hey, what if we put these together and see what falls out.

The other part was resources, which sounds mundane but completely changes what questions you're even willing to ask. In academia, if an experiment is going to take two weeks of your cluster allocation, you don't run it — you spend that time thinking of a cheaper proxy. At OpenAI the attitude was much more, just run it, and run it at a scale where the answer is unambiguous. That shifts your taste. You start asking questions whose answers are only visible at scale, and some of those turn out to be the important ones.

And there was a real tolerance for things not working. Lots of projects died. Nobody treated that as a failure of the person. I think that's actually the hard thing to reproduce — not the compute, people talk about compute, but the willingness to let smart people spend six months on something that might be nothing.

If I'm being even-handed about it, there were tradeoffs. It was less reflective than academia in some ways — less time spent on the careful ablation, the "do we really understand why this works" question. There was a strong bias toward forward motion. And it was a very particular kind of person who thrived there; the lack of structure that I found liberating, other people found disorienting. But for that stretch, for the questions we were asking, it was about as good an environment as I could imagine.

r001.rationale: The response describes OpenAI as a research environment with resources to run large-scale experiments, but it does not characterize the organization as nonprofit.

sonnet-5.5.text:
It was a really special time to be there. I was at OpenAI in 2017 and 2018, when it was still quite small, maybe a few dozen researchers. It felt much more like a tight-knit lab than a company. Everyone knew what everyone else was working on, and you could walk over and talk to anyone, whether it was Ilya or Alec or someone on a completely different project.

What stood out most was how much freedom there was to pursue ideas you believed in, together with a strong sense of ambition. There were a few big efforts, like the RL work on games, and a lot of people were excited about those. But there was also room for smaller bets that didn't have a clear payoff yet. The language modeling work was one of those. At the time it wasn't the center of gravity for the organization, and I don't think any of us expected it to become what it did.

The other thing I'd say is that the culture was very empirical and very focused on what actually works. It was less about writing the perfect theoretical argument and more about "let's try this, scale it up, and see what happens." Coming from academia, where I was used to thinking carefully about a problem and designing a method for it, that was a real shift. You could just run the experiment, and if the signal was there, you'd keep pushing on it.

Having access to good compute and strong engineering support also made a big difference. It let us iterate on ideas much faster than I could have in a typical academic setting. Looking back, I think that combination of a small team, freedom to explore, and a willingness to bet on simple ideas at scale is what made that environment so productive.

r001.rationale: The response describes OpenAI as a small, tight-knit lab and mentions good compute and engineering support, but it does not characterize it as well-funded or mention its nonprofit status.
